prompt.context: A major East Coast, vertically integrated and regulated electric utility has received a permit to build its first nuclear power plant. It wants to know if this will be a good investment and possible risks associated with this venture.
prompt.question: Should the utility go ahead with building the nuclear power plant? Is it a good investment, and what are the associated risks?

clarifying_info.q: Can you describe the structure of the company? What does 'vertically integrated' and 'regulated' mean?
clarifying_info.a: A vertically integrated utility owns the entire value chain – generation, transmission and distribution. It is somewhat of a monopoly and is overseen by state regulators.
There is virtually no competition because it is a regulated industry.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the plant?
clarifying_info.a: The new plant is expected to supply about 8,760 GWh (Gigawatt hours) per year and it is expected to be utilized for 30 years.
The current annual demand in the utility's service area is 17,000 GWh. For this case assume this demand will remain constant in the near future.

clarifying_info.q: What is the expected revenue on a variable basis?
What is the expected variable cost?
Why is the utility building this new plant?
clarifying_info.a: Currently the company has about 9,000 GWh of supply that comes from old, dirty and inefficient coal fired power plants. It plans to retire them in the near future.
The utility plans to outsource the building of the nuclear plant and the price quote is about $7 Billion.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market cap of our client?
clarifying_info.a: The market cap of this company is $6 Billion.

framework: Understand the company structure and industry: regulated monopoly, full value chain ownership, no competition
Evaluate the cost of the investment: quoted cost plus expected value of cost overruns
Calculate contribution margin and annual contribution from the plant
Determine the breakeven period and compare to industry benchmarks
Assess financial risks: investment size vs. market cap, financing requirements, capital constraints
Assess organizational risks: specialized personnel, training, safety and reliability

questions.prompt: What is the expected value (EV) of the total construction cost, accounting for cost overrun risk?
questions.guidance: Candidate should add probability-weighted overrun costs to the base quoted cost of $7B. Key insight: the expected fixed cost exceeds the entire market cap of the company ($6B).

math.setup: Base cost $7B. Three components each carry overrun risk: Technology & engineering ($4B base, 50% chance of $800M overrun), Structure ($2B base, 50% chance of $600M overrun), Other overhead ($1B base, 20% chance of $250M overrun).

questions.prompt: What is the annual contribution margin from the plant?
questions.guidance: Candidate must convert units carefully (GWh to MWh) to compute contribution per unit, then scale to full plant capacity.

math.setup: Plant capacity: 8,760 GWh/year. Revenue: $80/MWh. Variable cost: $10/MWh. Note: 1 GWh = 1,000 MWh.

questions.prompt: What is the breakeven period for this investment?
questions.guidance: Divide the expected total fixed cost by annual contribution. Compare the result to the industry average breakeven of 6–7 years to highlight the unfavorable economics.

math.answer: Approximately 13 years, roughly twice the industry average of 6–7 years

questions.prompt: What are the key financial and organizational risks of proceeding?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates proactively raise: (1) investment cost ($7.75B) exceeds market cap ($6B), forcing heavy debt or expensive equity; (2) 13-year payback ties up capital and crowds out other investments; (3) shortage of nuclear-qualified personnel; (4) training, safety, and reliability demands; (5) regulatory change risk during a long construction horizon.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks should the client consider before proceeding with this investment?

categories.name: Financial risks
ideas: Investment cost ($7.75B) exceeds market cap ($6B) – existential capital risk
Must rely heavily on debt or expensive equity to finance the plant
Long payback (~13 years vs. 6–7 year industry average) ties up capital
Limited capacity for other capital investments during payback period
Construction cost overruns increase exposure beyond base case

categories.name: Organizational / operational risks
ideas: Shortage of personnel with nuclear plant operating skills
Significant training and hiring costs for specialized workforce
Safety and reliability requirements for nuclear technology are stringent
First nuclear plant – no internal experience or institutional knowledge
Complex technology raises operational risk and potential downtime

categories.name: Regulatory risks
ideas: Regulatory environment could change (e.g., stricter nuclear rules, rate reviews)
Long construction timeline increases exposure to policy shifts
Permitting and compliance requirements may add cost or delay

categories.name: Strategic / market risks
ideas: Plant life of 30 years locks client into nuclear technology long-term
Current demand (17,000 GWh) exceeds retiring coal (9,000 GWh) – supply shortfall if project delayed
Alternative generation technologies (gas, renewables) may become cheaper
Public sentiment toward nuclear could shift

recommendation: The client should NOT proceed with this investment at this time.
The expected construction cost of $7.75B exceeds the company's $6B market cap, creating an existential financial risk.
The breakeven period of ~13 years is roughly twice the industry average of 6–7 years, meaning capital will be tied up for an unusually long time.
risks: Heavy reliance on debt or dilutive equity to finance a project larger than the company itself
Crowding out of all other capital investments for over a decade
Shortage of skilled nuclear personnel and high training/safety costs
Regulatory changes over the long construction and payback horizon
Construction cost overruns could push the total well beyond $7.75B
next_steps: Evaluate less expensive generation technologies (natural gas, renewables) to replace the retiring coal plants with a shorter payback period
Model alternative financing scenarios and assess debt covenant / credit-rating implications
Explore partnership or co-investment structures to share the capital burden
Review regulatory landscape for evolving nuclear policy before making a final decision
